extracted.intended_audience: patent researchers, IP scholars, policymakers, and patent-quality analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Use empirical baselines and application-level markers to evaluate the likelihood that a US patent application will be granted and to interpret an issued patent's quality signal. Focuses on per-application allowance rates, continuation practices, art-unit and examiner allowance behavior, and entity-size effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-application overall allowance rate (baseline prior)
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical per-application allowance rate across the sample (1996–mid-2013) is 55.8%. This is the baseline prior probability that an individual USPTO application will be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 55.8% as the prior probability against which individual patent grants should be assessed; deviations by technology, art unit, examiner, or applicant characteristics should condition this prior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-adjusted allowance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: When continuations are counted as creating new applications, the effective per-application grant rate rises (authors estimate ~71%) because applicants who fail can refile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish per-invention and per-application rates: counting continuation-children as separate applications changes the interpretation of grant likelihood and can reveal strategic refiling behavior that inflates apparent success.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-action allowance probability (technology variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that an application is allowed on first action varies dramatically by technology area (the 'first-action allowance probability' is technology-dependent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition expectations of first-action allowance on the application's technology class; some technologies historically see much lower or higher first-action allowances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-specific allowance trends (declines/increases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance rates changed over time differently by technology; e.g., substantial declines in 'Drugs and Medical Instruments' and 'Computers and Communications' (especially after Bilski/Mayo/Alice), while other classes remained more stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret a grant in the context of temporal trends for its technology: patents issued during periods of declining allowance rates are likely more rigorously vetted; those issued during rising rates may reflect policy or practice laxity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm-size / entity-size effect on grant rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications from small entities had lower grant rates than large entities. This reflects prosecution sophistication, application quality investment, and repeat-player knowledge differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust quality inferences for entity size: grants to small entities can indicate a higher passing bar (selection effect), while grants to large entities may include marginal applications facilitated by superior prosecution; consider entity size when comparing patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance rate of the assigned art unit as a comparative quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The art unit's historical allowance rate normalizes for examiner-pool laxity: a grant from a low-allowance-rate art unit is, all else equal, a stronger quality signal than one from a high-allowance-rate unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a patent's issuance against its art unit's baseline allowance rate; lower art-unit rates increase the weight of a grant as evidence of substantive patentability. Example: software business-method art units (e.g., 3622, 3624) historically had low allowance rates, so grants there signal stronger patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner-level allowance rate relative to art-unit median
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's individual allowance rate compared to the art-unit median provides another normalization: grants by lower-allowing examiners are stronger signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a granted patent, evaluate the granting examiner's allowance rate against the art-unit median — an allowance from an examiner with a lower-than-median rate implies a stronger signal of patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation practice as a quality/selection marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a patent was issued via continuation chains or without continuations affects its signal: continuations can reflect applicant persistence rather than underlying invention quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat patents issued after long continuation activity or after parent abandonment with skepticism about intrinsic quality; patents issued without RCEs or continuations are stronger signals of underlying patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-action notice of allowance (application-level marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the application receive a notice of allowance on first action? This is an application-level marker but is a mixed signal: it could indicate high application quality or weak examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret first-action allowance cautiously: corroborate with art-unit/examiner allowance rates and other markers (e.g., continuation history) before inferring high-quality patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of RCEs filed (response to examiner pushback)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many Requests for Continued Examination (RCEs) were filed — more RCEs indicate greater examiner pushback during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use RCE count as an indicator of how much negotiation/narrowing occurred; a higher number suggests more difficulty obtaining allowance and potentially weaker original claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-chain length to issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the continuation chain leading to issuance — longer chains may signal weaker underlying patentability or persistent prosecution effort to overcome rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long continuation chains should reduce confidence in the intrinsic quality of the ultimately issued patent, absent other corroborating signals (e.g., low art-unit allowance rate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-issuance relative to art-unit median
rubrics_metrics.description: Time from filing to issuance compared to the art-unit median: faster issuance may reflect weak examination, whereas slower issuance may indicate applications that required more substantial work or narrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare time-to-issuance to peers in the same art unit: unusually fast grants can be suspect; unusually slow grants may reflect either contentious prosecution or thorough vetting depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro-period indicators of rigor (period of declining vs. rising allowance rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a patent was issued during a period when the art-unit allowance rate was declining (more rigorous) or rising (more lax) conditions the inferred rigor of examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a grant in its macro temporal context: patents issued during widespread declines in allowance rates (e.g., post-major court decisions) are likelier to be rigorously examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological classification of applications (allowed/abandoned/pending and counting continuation-children as distinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's methodology treats each application as allowed, abandoned, or pending and counts continuation-children as distinct applications to compute true per-application success rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For empirical measures of grant probability, adopt the same counting conventions (treat continuation-children as separate) to avoid conflating per-invention and per-application measures; be explicit about the unit of analysis when comparing rates.
